subject: business-studies
title: PESTLE Foundations Adventure
welcome_lead: You'll meet PESTLE — political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors.
meta_desc: GCSE Business Studies external influences — the PESTLE framework explained.
final_note: You can list and define each PESTLE factor and give a real example of each.

concepts.def: Government policy and stability affecting business
New tech that creates or destroys markets
Laws on employment, consumers, the environment

walkthroughs.body_html:
PESTLE helps firms spot threats and opportunities outside their control.

If they ignore it, they may launch in a shrinking market or break new laws.
P: Brexit changing trade rules. E: rising interest rates. S: ageing population. T: AI tools. L: minimum wage rise. En: single-use plastic bans.
Firms react by adjusting strategy: cut costs in a recession, invest in tech to stay competitive, switch suppliers to meet new laws.

mcqs.q: An ageing population is which PESTLE factor?
options: Political
Economic
Social
Legal

mcqs.q: A government raising the minimum wage is which factor?
options: Technological
Environmental
Legal
Social

mcqs.q: Does a rise in the minimum wage only affect businesses badly?
options: A higher minimum wage can only harm businesses.
It raises labour costs, but it can also boost worker motivation and increase consumer spending power, and it applies equally to competitors.
The minimum wage is set separately by each business.
Exchange rates are the prices charged for exchanging faulty goods.

mcqs.q: Are exchange rates only relevant to giant multinationals?
options: No — small firms importing materials, or selling to tourists and online customers abroad, are affected by currency movements too.
Exchange rates are the prices charged for exchanging faulty goods.
Exchange rates don't matter unless a firm owns overseas factories.
Businesses can legally opt out of technological change.

mcqs.q: Is new technology always an opportunity for existing businesses?
options: Exchange rates are the prices charged for exchanging faulty goods.
Technological change benefits every established firm.
No — it can cut costs and open markets, but it can also make products obsolete, enable new competitors and require costly investment to keep up.
Businesses can legally opt out of technological change.
